description: To show that we live in a beautiful world
summary:
NASA’s Earth Information Center produces striking visualizations of our changing planet, but they are almost entirely visual, which leaves blind and low-vision people out. Earth Jukebox is a web app that translates those visuals into sound in real time, with no install and no account.

You choose an EIC-style visualization, such as sea surface temperature, sea ice, CO₂, forest height, night lights or lightning. A playhead then scans the frame from left to right. Color maps to pitch: warm hues play high notes and cool hues play low ones, snapped to a musical scale so the result stays pleasant rather than noisy. Brightness controls loudness, and six latitude bands play six separate voices, with the poles in the highest register. A year slider changes the data, and as the average warms, the music gets faster and tenser, shifts to a minor scale and drifts out of tune. That lets you hear climate change as well as see it.

The app is built with plain HTML, JavaScript, canvas pixel analysis and the Web Audio API, so it runs entirely in the browser. The built-in maps are stylized stand-ins modeled on EIC datasets (ocean temperature, ice, CO₂, vegetation, forest height, lightning and night lights). Real NASA frames are loaded by the user, and the same translation rules apply to them.

Live demo: https://adorable-chebakia-8f2ad0.netlify.app/
NASA data and visualizations: NASA Earth Information Center and Scientific Visualization Studio (svs.gsfc.nasa.gov)
details:
Earth Jukebox is a browser app that turns NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into music in real time. You pick a map, such as sea surface temperature, polar sea ice, atmospheric CO₂, forest height, night lights or lightning, and press play. A playhead sweeps the frame from left to right, and the app reads the pixels under it and turns them into sound:

  • Color becomes pitch. Warm hues play higher notes and cool hues lower ones, snapped to a pentatonic scale so the result stays musical.
  • Brightness becomes loudness. Gray areas such as land or missing data stay silent.
  • Latitude becomes voices. Six latitude bands play six separate voices, with the polar bands in the highest register, and stereo pan follows the playhead.
  • Warming becomes urgency. A year slider (1980–2050) changes the data. As the average warms, the tempo speeds up, the scale shifts to minor and the notes drift out of tune.

Users can also click, tap, drag or use the arrow keys to hear any single spot. Each spot is announced as text (latitude, longitude and value), and any real EIC frame can be dropped, pasted or uploaded and sonified with the same rules.

Benefits

  • Blind and low-vision users can reach EIC science that is otherwise visual only.
  • Sound can reveal patterns the eye skims past, such as gradients, edges and change over time.
  • It works in any browser with no install, no account and no data sent anywhere.
  • It suits classrooms, museums and outreach as a second way into the data.

Intended impact

The goal is to make Earth science more inclusive and more emotionally engaging. Hearing a planet warm up, with the music getting faster and tenser, makes climate data feel immediate. We want it to start conversations in schools, newsrooms and science centers, and to be one small step toward every NASA visualization also coming with a sound.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages and tools: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the Canvas API for pixel analysis, and the Web Audio API for real-time synthesis. It runs entirely in the browser with no backend or hardware.
  • Data and sources: NASA’s Earth Information Center and Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS 3912, 5313, 4950, 5011, 5196 and others) for the visualizations and the types of data the app handles.
  • Built-in maps: these are generated procedurally in the browser and modeled on those datasets, so they are stand-ins rather than NASA data. Real frames are loaded by the user.
  • Development: an AI assistant helped write and iterate on the code. [Edit this line to match your team’s actual use and the event’s AI disclosure rules.]
  • Hosting: Netlify.

How it is creative

  • It treats an image as a score: the picture is the sheet music and the playhead is the performer.
  • The mapping balances science and music. A raw pixel-to-sound translation would be noise, so pitches are snapped to a scale and each latitude band gets its own voice, making the output listenable while still following the data.
  • The warming effect is artistic as well as technical. Climate change is heard as tension, with faster tempo, minor mode and detuning, not just read off a chart.
  • The “jukebox” idea is playful and exploratory, so people can poke around the planet by ear.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility first: keyboard and touch exploration, screen-reader text, high-contrast light and dark themes, and no dependence on sight.
  • Musicality versus accuracy: we limited the pitch range and used a pentatonic scale so it stays pleasant, while keeping the direction of change (warmer is higher, brighter is louder) consistent and explainable.
  • Honesty about data: we state clearly that the built-in maps are stylized stand-ins and that real NASA frames can be loaded.
  • Ease of use: it needs no setup and runs offline once loaded, which helps classrooms and low-bandwidth settings.
  • Performance: frames are downsampled and each moment reads only one column of pixels, so it runs smoothly on phones.
